title: 2 Samuel 16:5–14
context: At Bahurim, Shimei, a man of Saul's family, curses David, throws stones, and calls him a man of blood whom the LORD is now repaying for Saul's house. Abishai offers to kill him, but David refuses, saying that if the LORD has told Shimei to curse, no one should stop him. David hopes that the LORD will see his distress and repay him with good. The scene raises deep questions about how God's purposes relate to human wickedness.

verses.text: When King David came to Bahurim, behold, a man of the family of Saul’s house came out, whose name was Shimei, the son of Gera. He came out and cursed as he came.
verses.arminianNotes: Shimei, of Saul's family, comes out cursing at Bahurim. Arminian readers see lingering resentment over Saul's fall finding an outlet, a man freely choosing to attack the king in his weakness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Shimei's resentment reveals unresolved loyalties to Saul's house. God's discipline of David now comes through a hostile voice, and David's response will show his heart.

verses.text: He cast stones at David and at all the servants of King David, and all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left.
verses.arminianNotes: Shimei throws stones at David and his servants, though mighty men surround the king. Arminian readers note Shimei's reckless courage, emboldened by David's apparent defeat.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the humiliation of the scene: the king who killed Goliath is stoned by a single man. God's discipline humbles David in ways that strip away any pretense of power.

verses.text: Shimei said when he cursed, “Be gone, be gone, you man of blood, and wicked fellow!
verses.arminianNotes: "Be gone, be gone, you man of blood." Arminian readers note that the charge may refer to deaths connected with Saul's house, though David was not guilty of them; the accusation also echoes David's real guilt in Uriah's death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that Shimei's specific charge about Saul's house is unjust, yet David knows he is a man of blood in another sense, through Uriah's murder (12:9). False words can carry painful truth.

verses.text: The LORD has returned on you all the blood of Saul’s house, in whose place you have reigned! The LORD has delivered the kingdom into the hand of Absalom your son! Behold, you are caught by your own mischief, because you are a man of blood!”
verses.arminianNotes: Shimei claims the LORD is repaying David for Saul's house. Arminian readers note that Shimei misreads God's purposes, attributing David's troubles to the wrong cause while claiming to speak for God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Shimei's theology is partly wrong but not entirely. God is indeed disciplining David, though for Uriah and Bathsheba (12:10–12), not for Saul's house.

verses.text: Then Abishai the son of Zeruiah said to the king, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Please let me go over and take off his head.”
verses.arminianNotes: Abishai offers to "take off his head." Arminian readers see the instinct to defend honor by violence, an instinct David will refuse, choosing restraint over retaliation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the sons of Zeruiah were often too harsh for David (3:39). Abishai's offer represents the way of the sword, which David sets aside in favor of submitting to God.

verses.text: The king said, “What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah? Because he curses, and because the LORD has said to him, ‘Curse David,’ who then shall say, ‘Why have you done so?’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: "The LORD has said to him, 'Curse David.'" Arminian readers usually take this as David's humble reading of events: God permits Shimei's cursing and David accepts it as deserved discipline, without making God the author of Shimei's malice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often see here God's sovereign ordering of even wicked acts. As in Genesis 50:20, a person means evil, but God directs it to his good purpose, while Shimei remains fully responsible. Both traditions agree that Shimei acts wickedly and is responsible, and that David responds with humility.

verses.text: David said to Abishai and to all his servants, “Behold, my son, who came out of my bowels, seeks my life. How much more this Benjamite, now? Leave him alone, and let him curse; for the LORD has invited him.
verses.arminianNotes: "Leave him alone, and let him curse; for the LORD has invited him." Arminian readers see David accepting suffering with humility, a contrast to his son's grasping and his nephew's violence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David compares Shimei's cursing to his own son's betrayal. If God is disciplining him through Absalom, David can receive Shimei's words as part of the same discipline.

verses.text: It may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me, and that the LORD will repay me good for the cursing of me today.”
verses.arminianNotes: "It may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me." Arminian readers see hope in God's mercy: David trusts that God may yet respond to his humility with good.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David leaves vindication to God. His hope is not in silencing Shimei but in God's gracious character, which can turn cursing into blessing.

verses.text: So David and his men went by the way; and Shimei went along on the hillside opposite him and cursed as he went, threw stones at him, and threw dust.
verses.arminianNotes: Shimei follows along the hillside, cursing, throwing stones and dust. Arminian readers note David's sustained restraint, a picture of patience under provocation that requires repeated choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David endures without retaliation. Shimei's fate is settled later (1 Kings 2:8–9), but for now David entrusts the matter to God's justice.

verses.text: The king and all the people who were with him arrived weary; and he refreshed himself there.
verses.arminianNotes: The king and his people arrive weary and refresh themselves. Arminian readers see God's quiet provision of rest after a day of grief, humiliation, and endurance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God grants refreshment to his weary servant. The day's troubles end in rest, a small sign of God's care in the midst of discipline.
